item.content:encoded:
If you’ve been setting up MCP connections or agentic workflows, this release is for you. You ask an AI tool to check your site’s SEO. It comes back with real findings: a product page that’s telling Google it’s a recipe, a link still pointing to an old test version of your site. Helpful, but useless on its own: you still have to go and fix each one yourself, by hand, in the back end of your website. Now, Yoast SEO enables the same AI tool to make those changes for you.

Yoast SEO Abilities is what makes that possible. It lets your AI tool read what’s wrong with a page’s SEO and update it directly, the same technical settings you’d otherwise have to change by hand. You diagnose and fix in the same place.

AI tools are moving from answering questions to being able to take actions. Abilities gives that shift a front door on your own site, one you control.

What you could do before 

Since its release in April, Yoast SEO already registers three abilities with WordPress’s Abilities API: SEO scores, readability scores, and inclusive language scores for your most recently modified posts. Any AI tool could reliably check which posts had a weak SEO score. However, it had no standardized way to read the underlying fields or change them. Someone still had to open wp-admin. 

That gap is what this release closes. 

Read a post’s full SEO field set 

yoast-seo/get-post-seo-data returns the title, meta description, robots flags, schema type, canonical, social previews, and scores. 

In addition, you can identify the post by ID, permalink, or title search. As a result, your agent can find the post you mean from a plain-language description in one call, instead of hunting through several. 

Fix the technical fields 

Core technical settings are now writable from your AI tool: canonical, robots flags, cornerstone, and schema type. These are fields Yoast already manages, so nothing new sits between your content and your site. 

Roll back what you change 

Any change made through the WordPress Abilities API can be rolled back, as long as your AI tool holds the changed values in context. In practice, read a post’s SEO data before you update it. Then stay in that session while you review the result. Once the context is gone, the previous value goes with it, so treat the read call as part of the write. 

Work in bulk 

Bulk and batch operations let you apply a get, update, or filter request across multiple posts in one call. You get per-post results back, so you can see exactly what changed and where. 

Control where it matters 

Your focus keyphrase stays read-only. You always set it yourself, and it is never generated for you. An automatic change there could invalidate content briefs or marketing workflows, and it would skew every assessment that follows. For content workflows, we suggest continuing in the editor, where the content flow lives. 

Access follows native WordPress capability checks. There is no separate permission system to learn. Therefore, you can audit access the same way you audit any other admin-level access. 

Built on WordPress standards 

These abilities use WordPress’s Abilities API. Once you connect the WordPress MCP Adapter, they become callable MCP tools for any MCP-aware client, for example Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, or VS Code. Therefore no custom integration is needed. 

Typed input and output schemas spell out what to send and what to expect back. For anyone building dashboards or reporting tools on top, that predictability matters more than any single feature. 

For agencies, it also means one standard setup across every WordPress build, with no manual per-site reconfiguration. 

What you need to get started 

Connect your own LLM subscription to Yoast first. After that, read access, core SEO field updates, and bulk operations are all included as part of Yoast SEO. The developer documentation covers the full ability list, the typed input and output schemas, and how to connect the WordPress MCP Adapter. 

See it in your dashboard

Once you’ve connected your LLM subscription, head to Yoast SEO, then Integrations. We’ve also reorganized this page: instead of one long list, integrations are now grouped by topic, so they’re easier to scan. Look for the new AI & agentic group. For further information, read the help article on how to set up Abilities.

item.title: A prompting guide for AI website builders
item.dc:creator: Camille Cunningham
item.description:
AI website builders make it possible to go from a blank screen to a live website in minutes. Which is a great option if you want to get your website live, but don’t have the technical skills to get this done yourself. But there’s a catch most people run into: type in a vague prompt, […]

The post A prompting guide for AI website builders appeared first on Yoast.
item.content:encoded:
AI website builders make it possible to go from a blank screen to a live website in minutes. Which is a great option if you want to get your website live, but don’t have the technical skills to get this done yourself. But there’s a catch most people run into: type in a vague prompt, you will get a generic result.

The prompt “Build me a website for my bakery” will get you a website. But it won’t get you your website. The one you envisioned with your style, brand colors, tone of voice, layout and the features needed to cater to your (online) customers.

The good news is that this is fixable, and it doesn’t require any technical skill. It requires learning to prompt like briefing a designer. Instead of throwing your request out there and hoping to get lucky with what the builder comes up with.

Why basic prompts produce generic websites

AI site builders, like Bluehost’s AI-powered website builder, are a powerful tool to create websites. However, they work by filling in any gaps themselves. If you don’t specify your industry, tone, brand, or features, the AI builder is left to their own devices. It will have to guess. And it guesses whatever is statistically average for a site like yours. That’s why a lot of AI-generated sites feel interchangeable: the same banner, same stock photography, and the same layout you’ve run into a thousand times already. 

The more specific and structured your prompt, the less guessing the AI tool has to do. Which increases the chance of output reflecting your actual business and features needed. 

The 5 parts of a well-thought out prompt

I will share a few examples of prompts that you can use to build your website. But before I do, it helps to know what a strong prompt actually consists of. You will probably not need all five in every prompt, but the best prompts usually contain the majority of them: 

  • Who you are and what you do: your business type, niche, and what makes you different.
  • Who the site is for: your target visitor and what they’re trying to accomplish.
  • The pages and structure you need: the page hierarchy, type of pages needed and what goes on them.
  • Tone and style: how you want it to feel and look (if you have a logo and/or brand guide, you can also include this)
  • Functionality: the specific features that make the site actually work (booking forms, online ordering, galleries, contact forms, newsletter signups).

Real example prompts to copy and adapt

Example 1: A local service business (landscaping company)

Weak prompt: 

“Make a website for my landscaping business.” 

Strong prompt: 

“Build a website for a residential landscaping company called Greenery Design, serving homeowners in the Denver metropolitan area. The tone should be trustworthy and down-to-earth, not flashy. Think reliable neighbor, not luxury brand. Include a homepage with a strong hero section featuring a call-to-action for a free quote, a services page listing lawn care, garden design, irrigation installation, and seasonal cleanup, a photo gallery page to showcase before-and-after project photos, an about page introducing the owner and crew, and a contact page with a quote request form that asks for name, phone number, property size, and service needed. Use earthy greens and browns in the color palette, and make sure the quote form is visible on every page, not just the contact page.” 

Example 2: A personal portfolio (freelance photographer)

Weak prompt: 

“Create a portfolio site for a photographer.” 

Strong prompt: 

“Design a portfolio website for a freelance wedding and portrait photographer named Alina Barr. The site should feel elegant, warm, and editorial. Like a high-end wedding magazine, with lots of white space and large full-bleed photos rather than small thumbnails. Structure it with a homepage that opens on a full-screen image slideshow, a portfolio page organized into three categories (weddings, engagements, portraits), an about page written in first person with a friendly, personal tone, a pricing/packages page with three tiers, and a contact page with a simple inquiry form asking for event date, location, and event type. Use a serif font for headings and a clean sans-serif for body text, and keep the color palette neutral: cream, black, and a soft blush accent.” 

Example 3: A small ecommerce shop (handmade candles)

Weak prompt: 

“I need an online store for my candle business.” 

Strong prompt: 

“Build an ecommerce website for a small handmade candle brand called Amber & Ash. The vibe should be cozy and artisanal, with warm, moody photography and a rustic-meets-modern feel. Include a homepage that highlights the bestselling scent collection and a short brand story, a shop page with product categories for seasonal scents, everyday scents, and gift sets, individual product pages with scent notes, burn time, and size options, an FAQ page covering shipping, returns, and candle care tips, and a newsletter signup offering 10% off a first order. The checkout should be simple and mobile-friendly, since most customers will be shopping from their phones. Use a warm neutral palette (terracotta, cream, and charcoal) and avoid anything that looks too corporate or minimalist.” 

Example 4: A nonprofit or community organization

Weak prompt: 

“Make a website for our nonprofit.” 

Strong prompt: 

“Create a website for a nonprofit called Community Roots Youth Network, which provides after-school tutoring and mentorship for middle and high school students in underserved communities. The tone should be hopeful and human-centered, using lots of photos throughout the website. Structure the site with a homepage that leads with our mission statement and a prominent donate button, a programs page describing our tutoring, mentorship, and college-prep initiatives separately, an impact page with a few key statistics and short quotes from families we’ve helped, a volunteer page with a sign-up form, and a donate page with suggested giving amounts. Make the donate button sticky in the navigation bar so it’s visible from every page, and use a color palette of deep blue and warm yellow to feel both trustworthy and optimistic.” 

Example 5: A consultant or coach (business strategy consultant)

Weak prompt: 

“Build a website for my consulting business.” 

Strong prompt: 

“Design a website for an independent business strategy consultant named Ann Reyes, who works with small business owners on growth planning and operations. The tone should be confident and professional but approachable, not stiff or corporate. Include a homepage with a clear one-sentence explanation of who I help and how, a services page breaking down three offerings (one-time strategy sessions, monthly advising retainers, and workshop facilitation), each with a short description and price range, a case studies page with two or three short client success stories, an about page focused on my background and philosophy, and a contact page with a ‘Book a Free Consultation’ button linked to a calendar scheduling tool. Use a navy and gold color scheme, and keep the overall layout clean and uncluttered, with plenty of white space.” 

Quick prompting checklist

Use the examples above to write your own detailed prompt. But before you hit ‘generate’ it can’t hurt to run your prompt past this checklist: 

  • Have I named my business/brand and described what it actually does? 
  • Have I described who visits the site and what they want to do there? 
  • Have I listed the specific pages and site structure I need, not just “a website”? 
  • Have I described the tone or feeling I want? 
  • Have I given any color or style direction? 
  • Have I called out any must-have features/functionalities? 
  • Are there files I can include to guide the tool in more detail, such as logos, brand guides, a mission statement, (product) photos? Make sure any files that you include are allowed to be shared externally.  

Don’t be afraid to iterate

One of the biggest advantages of AI website builders is that the first result doesn’t have to be the final one. Treat your first prompt as a rough draft and refine from there. If the homepage feels too busy, tell the AI directly: “Simplify the homepage: remove the testimonials section and make the hero image larger.” If the tone feels off, say so: “This feels too formal, make the copy warmer and more conversational.” 

That being said, do start out with a strong prompt. This not only saves the website builder a lot of resources, it also helps you get a clear idea of what you want and tweak instead of build from scratch. The AI is a collaborator, not a mind reader. The clearer and more specific you are, in your first prompt and in every refinement after it, the closer your site will get to something that actually feels like yours. 

AI builders vs custom design

AI powered website builders are incredibly useful to get a website up and running in no time. But it is also good to be aware of its limitations and the added value of hiring an expert to set up your website. A website designer or agency has experience with what works well and what doesn’t, and can come up with original ideas that exactly fit your needs. So if you have the time and funds to do so, consider this option and figure out what’s best for you. Especially if you need a more complex website or one that needs to be able to easily grow and have features added to it in the future. A human touch will always bring that unique touch to your website.

Also, on that note

This blog post aims to help you get the best result using an AI-powered website builder. Of course, as part of this, you can ask the builder to generate content and add photos to your website. But please, use these as placeholders until you’re happy with the structure and design. After that, be very critical of any content on there. Rewrite the text to reflect you and what your business does and use real photos or images that are on brand. These final touches are going to make the difference between just another website and your authentic, one-of-a-kind website.

item.content:encoded:
Whether you’re writing a new blog post or working on your product pages, chances are you’ll find yourself asking whether your page needs an image. The answer is always “Yes”. Images bring a page to life and contribute to your website’s SEO. Don’t worry; we’ll help you figure out where to find the right image and optimize it for SEO in no time.

Table of contents

  • On optimizing your images
  • Always use images
  • Getting your images in AI search results
  • Finding the right image
  • Preparing images for use in your article
  • Adding the image to your article
  • XML image sitemaps
  • Serving images via an image CDN
  • A summary of image SEO

Key takeaways

  • Images enhance your website’s appeal and boost SEO by helping search engines understand content better.
  • Optimize images by using high-quality visuals, descriptive file names, and appropriate formats like WebP or AVIF.
  • Include alt text for accessibility and SEO, but avoid keyword stuffing; it should accurately describe the image’s content.
  • Use structured data for images to improve visibility in AI-driven search results and image searches.
  • Implement responsive images, reduce file sizes, and consider using an image CDN to improve loading speeds and performance.

On optimizing your images

Images do more than make your content look good. They help search engines understand your pages, improve your chances of being discovered, and can even bring traffic from visual search.

This guide covers everything you need to optimize your images for SEO. You’ll find practical tips on choosing the right formats, writing alt text that works, and using structured data effectively. Follow these steps, and your images will start performing a lot better.

Always use images

Images, when used correctly, will help readers better understand your article. Or get a better idea of the product or service you’re offering. The old saying, “A picture is worth a thousand words” probably doesn’t apply to Google, but it’s true when you need to spice up 1,000 dull words, illustrate what you mean in a chart, or make your social media posts more enticing.

It’s a simple recommendation: add images to every article you write or page you create to make them more appealing. With the search landscape rapidly changing and not just relying on text anymore, adding visuals to your pages could improve the performance of those pages.

Visual search is part of the equation. With AI and other multimedia developments on the rise, optimizing your images (and videos, for that matter) makes it easier for search engines and people to find you. Pages with unique, high-quality images tend to see better engagement, with users staying longer.

Google Lens handles over 20 billion searches every month. Not optimizing your images for visual search, means you’re missing a huge opportunity to attract this traffic.

Google Images

Google Images helps people find visual content across the web. It displays images and organizes them by relevance, quality, and context. When you search, it shows thumbnails, but clicking an image can take you to the webpage where it’s hosted. For site owners, Google Images can be a source of traffic, as optimized images can rank here and bring visitors to your site. It also supports reverse image searches, letting users find similar images or locate where an image appears online.

Google Lens

Google Lens lets you search the world around you using just an image. Point your camera at an object, landmark, or product, and it identifies it, finds similar items, or even translates text in real time. For businesses, this means your images can drive traffic if they’re optimized right. To show up well in Lens, use high-quality, original images with clear alt text and structured data. Google matches what it sees in the image with what it knows about your page. Original, detailed images with clear metadata perform best, so avoid generic stock photos and focus on visuals that truly represent your content.

Getting your images in AI search results

AI search results, like Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, are changing how people find information. These systems use images to answer questions, so optimizing your visuals can help them appear in AI-generated responses.

The good news is that most image SEO best practices also apply to AI search. Clear, descriptive alt text helps AI understand your images, just as it helps screen readers. Structured data like ImageObject gives AI systems additional context to interpret and reference your visuals. High-quality, original images also perform better, just like they do in traditional search.

For the best results, focus on the same tactics you use for image SEO. Use detailed alt text, provide structured data, and ensure your images are high-quality and relevant. AI systems often draw on indexed images, so make sure your images are indexed in Google Images.

Check Google Search Console to see how your images perform. If your images are already optimized for SEO, you’re likely already prepared for AI search. Just keep refining these practices as AI continues to evolve.

Finding the right image

It’s always better to use original images, like high-quality photos you have taken, than stock photos. Your team page needs pictures of your actual team, not this man on the right or one of his other stock photo friends.

Your article needs an image relevant to its subject. If you’re adding a random photo just to get a green bullet in the Yoast SEO content analysis, you’re doing it wrong. The image should reflect the post’s topic or have illustrative purposes within the article. Also, try to place the image near the relevant text. If you have a central image or an image you’re trying to rank, try to keep that near the top of the page if possible without feeling forced. There is a simple image SEO reason for all of this. An image surrounded by relevant text gives Google more context, which helps it rank for related queries. We’ll go into image SEO later on.

Alternatives

Don’t have any original images you can use on your website? There are other ways to find unique images. Flickr: Creative Commons and Unsplash are great image sources, for instance, as you can use Creative Commons images. Remember to check out the restrictions and attribute the original photographer when you use one of their images. Our blog post gives you an overview of where to get great images.

Steer clear of obvious stock photos, but if you insist on using these, pick the ones that look more genuine. Whatever you use, you’ll probably find that images with people in them tend to look like stock photos. Unless you took the photos yourself, which, in our opinion, is always the best idea.

Apparent alternatives for photos are illustrations or graphs. Animated GIFs deserve a mention too. They’re everywhere these days.

Even though animated GIFs are popular, don’t overdo it. It’ll make your post more challenging to read, as the movement of the image distracts your readers’ attention. Also, not unimportant and good to mention is that they can slow down your page as the filesize can be huge.

Preparing images for use in your article

Once you’ve found the right image, like a photo, an illustration, or a chart, the next step is optimizing it for your website. Before you add your image, there are a few things you need to think about:

Choose the right file name

Image SEO starts with the file name. You would like Google to know what the image is about without even looking at it. So, use your focus keyphrase in the image file name. It’s simple: if you’re writing an article on the Notre Dame and use an image showing a sunrise in Paris over the Notre Dame Cathedral, the file name shouldn’t be DSC4536.jpg. A proper file name would be notre-dame-paris-sunrise.jpg. That way, the photo’s main subject (and perhaps your article) is at the beginning of the file name.

Choose the right format

For images, the right format doesn’t exist. It depends on the kind of image and how you want to use it. In short, we recommend to:

  • Choose WebP for larger photos or illustrations. It gives you good results for colors and clarity;
  • use PNG if you want to preserve background transparency in your image;
  • or use AVIF, as it will produce high-quality results with even smaller file sizes. In this case, you do need a WebP or JPEG fallback for browsers that don’t support the AVIF format. You can use tools like Squoosh to convert your image into the format you need.
  • use SVG for logos and icons. With the help of CSS or JavaScript, you can manage images in SVG format. For instance, resize them without loss of quality.

If you know a large part of your audience uses specific browsers or devices, check whether those browsers on CanIuse.com support your preferred format. When you’ve chosen the correct name and format, it’s time to resize and optimize your image!

Scale for image SEO

Loading times influence user experience and SEO. The faster the site, the easier for users and search engines to visit a page. Images can add to your loading times, especially when you upload a huge image to display it small, for example, a 2500×1500 pixel image displayed at 250×150 pixels size.

Even if it is displayed a lot smaller, the entire image still has to be loaded. So, resize the image to the size you want to display it. WordPress helps you do this by automatically providing images in multiple sizes after uploading them. Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean the file size is also optimized; that’s just the image display size. So think about the size in which you upload your images.

Use responsive images

Responsive images help your SEO. If you’re using WordPress, it’s done automatically by default. Images should have the srcset attribute, which makes it possible to serve a different image per screen width. This is especially useful for mobile devices.

Reduce file size

The next step in image SEO is to ensure your scaled image is compressed. That way, it’s served in the smallest file size possible. It is good to know that WordPress does compress the images you upload, but, unfortunately, this automatic compression often isn’t enough to rely on it alone.

Of course, you could export the image and experiment with quality percentages. We prefer to use the highest possible quality images, especially given the popularity of high-resolution screens in mobile and desktop devices.

You can still reduce the file size of these images by removing the EXIF data, for example. We recommend using tools like ImageOptim or websites like Squoosh, JPEGmini, jpeg.io or Kraken.io.

When you’ve optimized your images, you can test your page with tools like Google PageSpeed Insights, WebPageTest.org or Pingdom.

Improve LCP in Core Web Vitals

Setting width and height attributes on your images lets the browser reserve space before the image loads. This prevents layout shifts and improves your Core Web Vitals, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP).

When you define the width and height properties for images in CSS, the browser can allocate the required space for the image before it is fully loaded. This allows the browser to render the content more accurately and avoids unexpected layout shifts, which can be frustrating for users.

Here are some important benefits of doing this:

  1. Prevents layout shifts: By setting the exact dimensions of images, you reserve the appropriate space for them. This ensures that other content on the page doesn’t shift or jump around when the images load. Users can start consuming the content without distractions, leading to a better user experience.
  2. Improves page loading speed: When the browser knows the dimensions of an image in advance, it can allocate space for it while other page elements continue to load. This helps to optimize the page loading speed, particularly the LCP metric, as the largest contentful element’s space is reserved from the start.
  3. Optimizes browser rendering: Knowing the image dimensions allows the browser to perform better in rendering and painting. It can allocate resources efficiently and optimize the rendering pipeline, resulting in a smoother and faster browsing experience.

To specify width and height you can use either inline styles or external stylesheets for images in CSS. Here’s an example:

img {
  width: 500px; /* Set the desired width */
  height: 300px; /* Set the desired height */
}

Instead of using fixed pixel values, you can use relative units like percentages or viewport-based units (e.g., vw, vh) to make the image responsive and adapt to different screen sizes.

It’s important to note that specifying the dimensions in CSS only sets the image’s display size and not its actual file size. To optimize image file sizes for faster loading, consider compressing and resizing images before uploading them to your website.

Download priority

For the most important image on your page, the LCP image, add fetchpriority="high". This tells the browser to load it first, improving user experience and performance. For images that appear further down the page, add decoding="async". This lets the browser decode them in the background, so they don’t slow down the rest of your content.

By specifying these elements for your images in CSS, you improve your website’s overall performance, visual stability, and user experience. Combine this practice with other image SEO techniques, such as proper image formats, compression, and lazy loading, for maximum impact on your website’s speed and Core Web Vitals.

Adding the image to your article

While Google is improving at recognizing what’s in an image, you shouldn’t rely on their abilities yet. It all comes down to you providing the context for that image, so fill in as much as you can! We’ll discuss how below.

When your image is ready to use, don’t just throw it into your article anywhere. As mentioned earlier, adding it close to related textual content helps a lot. It makes sure the text is as relevant to the image as the image is to the text, something users and Google prefer.

Captions

The image caption is the text that accompanies the image on the page. If you look at the images here, it’s the text in the gray box below each one. Why are captions important for image SEO? People use them when scanning an article. People tend to scan headings, images and captions as they scan a web page. Way back in 1997, Jakob Nielsen wrote:

“Elements that enhance scanning include headings, large type, bold text, highlighted text, bulleted lists, graphics, captions, topic sentences, and tables of contents.”

Do you need to add captions to every image? No, because sometimes images serve other purposes. Decide whether you want to use yours for SEO as well or not. You should only add captions where it would make sense to the visitor for one to be there. Think about the visitor first, and don’t add a caption just for image SEO purposes.

alt text

The alt text (or alt tag) is added to an image, so descriptive text will be in place if the image can’t be displayed to the visitor for any reason. This is how Wikipedia puts it:

Alternative text (or alt text) is text associated with an image that serves the same purpose and conveys the same essential information as the image. In situations where the image is not available to the reader, perhaps because they have turned off images in their web browser or are using a screen reader due to a visual impairment, the alternative text ensures that no information or functionality is lost. Absent or unhelpful alternative text can be a source of frustration for visually impaired users.

The alt text is there to enhance your website’s accessibility, so be sure to add alt text to the images you use. Also, consider including the SEO keyphrase for that page if appropriate, but do not stuff the alt text of every image with keywords. Most importantly, describe what’s in the picture so search engines and people can understand it. The more relevant information surrounding an image, the more search engines deem this image important.

However, please remember that not every image needs an alt text. Instead, consider alt text as a part of your content and add it where it makes sense. For instance, if you have an image purely for decorative reasons, then that image doesn’t need an alt text. In this case, having an alt text doesn’t bring any value to your readers. On the other hand, if you use an image with a statistic, let’s say, the number of people who searched for ice cream last month, then this should be reflected in the alt text. You can find guidance for alt text in this W3’s article or check out our guide on optimizing alt text for search engines.

Use AI to generate alt text for your products

Writing alt text for every image can feel like a lot of work, especially if your site has hundreds of product images. That’s why we built Yoast AI Generate for image alt text. Available in Yoast WooCommerce SEO and Yoast SEO AI+, it generates relevant alt text for your product images right in the product editor or the Yoast SEO bulk editor, based on your product data. You always review and approve the suggestions, so you stay in control.

title text

Some browsers show the title text as a ‘tooltip’ when hovering over an image. Most desktop browsers show the title text as was intended. Images’ titles are similar, and many people who use titles copy the alt text. More and more people leave them out altogether, why is that? Here’s Mozilla’s take:

“title has a number of accessibility problems, mainly based around the fact that screen reader support is very unpredictable and most browsers won’t show it unless you are hovering with a mouse (so e.g. no access to keyboard users).”

Including supporting information in the main article text is better than attaching it to the image.

Read more: Read more about alt tag and title tag optimization »

Add image structured data

Where a bare <img> tag leaves search engines guessing, structured data makes images explicit: schema.org markup such as ImageObject, and the image property on types like Article or Product, tells search engines what an image shows and how it connects to the page. This matters more now that AI-driven search experiences select and cite images automatically.

The good news for WordPress users is that Yoast SEO handles most of this automatically: instead of outputting bare image URLs, it generates full ImageObject nodes, with captions, dimensions, and content URLs. These are all stitched together into a connected site-wide schema graph, attaching your featured image to the article schema and product images to your WooCommerce listings. Features like image licensing metadata (license and acquireLicensePage) aren’t included by default, but can be added through Yoast’s schema API filters.

Google has guidelines you need to follow if you want your images to it to understand your images. You can find them all in Google’s Structured Data General Guidelines. Read the developer documentation for Yoast’s use of ImageObject.

Want to learn more about structured data? Enroll in our free Structured data training course to learn more about adding structured data to your pages!

OpenGraph and social sharing

Earlier on, we mentioned using images for social sharing. If you add the following image tag to the <head> section in your page HTML like this:

<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/link-to-image.jpg" />

That will ensure the image is included in your share on Facebook or X. OpenGraph is also used for other social media platforms like Threads, Pinterest and LinkedIn. Even productivity software like Slack supports OpenGraph.

Yoast SEO has a Social media appearance section where you can set and, in the Premium version, even preview your social posts. Make sure to use a high-quality image, like the original image you used in the post, as social platforms often use higher quality/larger images.

XML image sitemaps

As a web developer, you might wonder about XML image sitemaps. We’d prefer to describe this as images in XML sitemaps. Google is clear about this:

Image sitemaps are a way of telling Google about other images on your site, especially those that we might not otherwise find (such as images your site reaches with JavaScript code). You can create a separate image sitemap or add image sitemap tags to your existing sitemap; either approach is equally fine for Google. Image sitemaps are based on generic sitemaps so the general sitemap best practices also apply to image sitemaps. We also recommend that you follow the general best practices for publishing images.

Now and then, people ask us about XML image sitemaps. We don’t generate these in our plugin but follow Google’s advice and include them in the page or post sitemaps. Just scroll down in our post sitemap and see we have added images to all our posts (there is a column just for that). Adding images to your XML sitemaps helps Google index your images, so be sure to do so for better image SEO.

Serving images via an image CDN

We all know CDNs as one of the most popular site speed optimizations. Some companies that provide CDNs also have a specific CDN for images. The image CDNs are built around basic tasks: to optimize your images and get them to your visitor as fast as possible. Running an image CDN can speed up image delivery a lot, because the images are optimized automatically and served from servers closer to your visitors

An image CDN lets you handle the transformation, optimization and delivery of images. You can determine what loads when and how that should work. For instance, your images can be converted on-the-fly to modern formats, and serve AVIF to browsers that support it, while falling back to WebP and then JPEG if needed, because these formats load much faster at equal or better quality.

There are many image CDNs to choose from, like Sirv, Cloudinary and Imagekit. Also, platforms like Cloudflare let you determine how to resize, reformat and serve images.

A summary of image SEO

Image SEO is the sum of a number of elements. With Google getting better at recognizing elements in images every day, it makes sense to make sure the image and its elements contribute to a good user experience as well as SEO. It would be foolish to try to kid Google.

Keep these things in mind when adding an image to an article:

  • Use high-quality, unique and relevant images that matches your text
  • Pick a good file name for your image
  • Use modern images formats like WebP and AVIF
  • Make sure image dimensions match the image size as displayed
  • Use srcset if possible
  • Reduce file size for faster loading
  • Specify width and height for your images
  • Add a caption, if appropriate, for easier scanning of the page
  • Use proper image alt text. No need for a title text
  • Add structured data to your images
  • Add OpenGraph and Twitter Card tags for the image
  • Use images in your XML sitemaps
  • Serving images via a CDN
  • Provide all the context you can!

Besides contributing to SEO and user experience, images can also be important in conversion. So don’t underestimate the importance of image SEO on your site!

item.content:encoded:
Good vibes can spark great ideas, and now they can even help you build a website. With vibe coding, you don’t need to start by writing lines of code. Instead, you tell AI what you want to create, refine the results through conversation, and watch your website take shape. While it won’t replace every aspect of traditional development, it’s opening the door for more people to bring their ideas online.

In this guide, we’ll explore what vibe coding is, how to build a website with it, and how it compares to traditional coding.

Table of contents

  • What’s the vibe around vibe coding?
  • What can you build with vibe coding?
  • How to vibe code a website in 5 steps
  • How to avoid the vibe coding doom loop
  • Vibe coding vs. traditional coding: What’s the difference?
  • Vibe coding a website: FAQs
  • Your prompts build the site. SEO helps people find it

What’s the vibe around vibe coding?

The term vibe coding was coined in February 2025 by computer scientist Andrej Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI and former AI leader at Tesla. He used it to describe a new way of building software: instead of writing code line by line, you simply explain what you want to create and let AI generate the technical implementation. In Karpathy’s words, you “say stuff, run stuff, and copy-paste stuff, and it mostly works.“

At its core, vibe coding is about shifting your role. Instead of acting as the developer who writes every line of code, you become the creative director. You describe your vision, review what the AI generates, ask for changes, and continue refining the result until it matches what you have in mind. Rather than focusing on syntax, frameworks, or debugging, your attention stays on the bigger picture: what you want to build and how it should work.

Overall, if I had to describe vibe coding in one sentence, “I’d say it feels less like programming and more like collaborating with an AI that speaks both your language and the language of code.“

What can you build with vibe coding?

Vibe coding isn’t limited to generating snippets of code. Today’s AI-powered tools can help you create everything from simple landing pages to complete websites, web applications, dashboards, and internal business tools!

With vibe coding, you can:

  • Build websites and landing pages faster. AI can generate layouts, content, and page structures from a simple prompt, helping you move from idea to first draft in minutes.
  • Start with ideas instead of code. Rather than thinking about HTML, CSS, or JavaScript, you focus on your goals, audience, and the experience you want to create.
  • Generate a complete website foundation. AI can create pages, navigation menus, sections, and design elements that you can build on.
  • Focus on creativity rather than the technical setup. Spend more time shaping your messaging, branding, and design while AI handles much of the repetitive work and offloads technical tasks.
  • Customize and iterate quickly. AI-generated websites can be refined through multiple iterations, allowing you to adjust layouts, content, and other design elements until they match your needs.
  • Explore different ways to present the same content. AI can quickly generate different design approaches for the same information, making it easier to compare options and find the one that works best for your audience.

    For example, you could ask AI to create three versions of the same interface: one with low-contrast colors, one with vibrant colors, and one with a dark-mode option.

Understanding vibe coding for building a website

When the concepts of vibe coding are applied to website design, it means you can converse with an AI platform and bring your vision to life online without worrying about complex concepts like HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or other programming languages. Simply explain your brand in plain English and let AI handle much of the technical work.

For example, you could prompt an AI with something like:

“Create a modern website for a local coffee shop with warm colors, an online menu, customer testimonials, and a contact form.”

This conversational approach makes website creation much more accessible, especially for entrepreneurs, freelancers, creators, and small business owners who have ideas but little or no coding experience.

That said, vibe coding doesn’t eliminate the need for human input. AI can generate a strong starting point, but creating a successful website still depends on having a clear goal, understanding your audience, and reviewing the output before going online.

Key benefits of vibe coding a website

Vibe coding is changing the way people approach website creation. Instead of spending weeks learning programming languages or waiting for a first draft, you can start with an idea and let AI help you bring it to life.

For anyone with a website idea, that shift means more time to focus on what they want to achieve and less time spent worrying about the technical details. Even experienced developers are embracing vibe coding for rapid prototyping and repetitive development tasks because it helps them move from concept to execution much faster.

Here are some of the biggest reasons why vibe coding is gaining momentum:

Launch ideas in hours, not weeks

Every website starts as an idea, but turning that idea into something people can visit has traditionally taken time. Vibe coding shortens that journey considerably. By describing your website in natural language, AI can generate a functional first draft in minutes. Instead of staring at a blank screen, you’re reviewing something tangible and deciding how to improve it. That faster start means you can validate ideas, collect feedback, and get your business online sooner.

Also read: New: Yoast AI Content Planner turns a blank post into a structured draft

Experiment and prototypes faster

One of the biggest advantages of vibe coding is how quickly it lets you test and refine ideas. Instead of spending days or weeks building a prototype from scratch, you can describe your vision in plain language and let AI generate a working first draft in minutes.

Whether you’re exploring different layouts, validating a business idea, or creating a website for a client, you can quickly experiment, gather feedback, and improve the result through conversation, making it easier to iterate before investing significant time or resources.

Iterate through conversations

Perhaps the biggest shift isn’t that AI writes code, it’s that building a website becomes a conversation.

Instead of manually editing every element, you can ask AI to redesign a section, rewrite your homepage copy, add a testimonials section, or make the layout feel more modern. Each prompt builds on the previous one, allowing your website to evolve naturally over time.

Can you really build a website using prompts?

The answer is yes, but it’s not because AI has replaced websites with something entirely new. Instead, it has changed how we build them.

Think of prompts as the new interface for website creation. Instead of dragging elements onto a page or writing HTML and CSS, you describe your business, goals, and the kind of website you want. Modern AI website builders then translate those instructions into a functional first draft, which you can continue refining through conversation.

Also read: Perfect prompts: 10 tips for AI-driven SEO content creation

That doesn’t mean prompting replaces creativity or strategy. AI can generate the website, but it still relies on your direction. The clearer your vision and the more context you provide, the closer the final website will be to what you imagined.

How to vibe code a website in 5 steps

Building a website with vibe coding isn’t about finding the perfect prompt; it’s about following the right process. The more clearly you communicate your goals and refine the results, the closer your website will be to what you originally envisioned.

Here’s a simple five-step framework to help you get started.

1. Define the purpose and style of your website

Before you open an AI website builder, spend a few minutes thinking about what you want to build. The better you define your vision, the better AI can translate it into a website.

Start by answering a few simple questions:

  • Who is the website for?
  • What do you want visitors to do?
  • How should your brand feel?
  • What pages or features do you need?

For example, instead of writing: “Build me a business website.”

Try something more descriptive:

“Create a modern website for a boutique coffee roastery. Use warm earth tones, clean typography, and large product images. Include a homepage, About page, online shop, customer reviews, and a contact form. The overall style should feel welcoming, premium, and easy to navigate.”

It explains the website’s purpose, functionality, and personality, which is important for launching as a brand or business that people are searching for.

Also read: What is search intent and why is it important for SEO?

2. Choose an AI website builder

Once you have a clear idea of the website you want to create, the next step is choosing the right AI website builder.

AI tools can support website development in different ways. For example, coding agents such as Claude Code offer specialized capabilities for building websites, but they typically require you to work in a development environment or via a command-line interface.

On the other hand, AI website builders offer a more accessible alternative: instead of working in a terminal or configuring a development environment, you can describe what you want through a conversational interface and start with a functional website that you can refine.

If you’re building a website with AI, the Bluehost AI Website Builder is a great place to start. It asks a few questions about your business, goals, and preferred style before generating a personalized website that you can continue to customize. Because it’s built into Bluehost’s hosting platform, you can go from idea to a live website without juggling multiple tools or worrying about technical setup.

From there, your role shifts from building pages manually to guiding AI toward the website you envision.

3. Write your first vibe prompt

Your first prompt lays the foundation for everything that follows, so it’s worth spending a little extra time getting it right.

This is where the idea of context engineering becomes useful. Rather than trying to cram every instruction into one clever prompt, think about the information AI needs to understand your project: what you’re building, who it’s for, how it should look and feel, what pages it needs, and what you want visitors to do.

You can build this context around:

  • your business or project
  • your target audience
  • your preferred design style
  • the pages you need
  • important features or functionality
  • your brand’s tone of voice

The key idea is simple: don’t focus on writing a clever prompt; focus on giving AI the context it needs to make good decisions. And as you continue vibe coding, you can add or refine that context through subsequent conversations rather than trying to get everything right in your first message.

4. Refine your website through conversation

Don’t expect your first prompt to produce the perfect website, and that’s completely normal. Vibe coding is an iterative process. Once AI generates the first version, continue the conversation by making small, focused improvements.

For example, you could ask AI to:

  • make the hero section more visually engaging
  • rewrite your homepage copy in a friendlier tone
  • replace placeholder images with a cleaner layout
  • add customer testimonials
  • improve the mobile experience
  • make the call-to-action button more prominent

Making one change at a time usually produces better results than asking AI to redesign the entire website in a single prompt. Think of each prompt as another design review. With every iteration, your website moves closer to the experience you originally imagined.

5. Review, publish, and keep improving

Before publishing your website, take some time to review everything AI has generated.

Check that the content accurately represents your business, all links and forms work correctly, and the design looks good on both desktop and mobile devices. This is also the perfect time to replace placeholder text, add your own images, and make sure the website reflects your brand.

Once you’re happy with the result, connect your custom domain and publish your website.

One of the biggest advantages of vibe coding is that the process doesn’t stop after launch. Need to add a new service, update your homepage, or create a landing page for a campaign? Simply return to the AI website builder, describe what you want, and continue refining your website through conversation instead of starting from scratch.

How to avoid the vibe coding doom loop

One of the biggest advantages of vibe coding is how quickly you can turn an idea into a working website. But as you continue refining your prompts, there’s a chance you’ll run into what’s commonly known as the vibe coding doom loop.

This happens when AI gets stuck trying to solve the same issue repeatedly without actually fixing it. It may suggest several “solutions,” but each one either introduces a new problem or brings you back to where you started. Instead of moving your website forward, you end up going in circles.

The doom loop usually happens when AI loses track of the bigger picture. This can occur if your original prompts are too vague, you keep changing your website’s direction midway through the process, or you request too many unrelated changes at once. As the conversation becomes more complex, the AI may struggle to connect all the pieces together, leading to inconsistent results.

How to fix this situation

The good news is that the vibe coding doom loop is usually avoidable. A few simple habits can help you keep AI on track and make the website-building process much smoother.

Get clarity on what you want

As mentioned earlier, context engineering is about giving AI the information it needs to make better decisions, rather than relying on increasingly elaborate prompts. Before asking AI to make changes, consider whether you’ve provided enough context about what you’re trying to achieve, who the website is for, and what you want the change to accomplish.

For instance, if you’re refining your homepage, explain the outcome you’re aiming for and provide relevant context about your audience, messaging, layout, or user experience. This gives AI a better basis for making the change and reduces the chances of it solving one problem while creating another.

Manage AI mistakes instead of chasing them

It’s important to remember that AI isn’t perfect. Treat each suggestion as a draft rather than a final answer. Google Trends adds comparison over time data

Guide to Preferred Sources in Google Search.

item.content:encoded:
The Yoast SEO Bulk Editor already helps you update titles, meta descriptions, and focus keyphrases across your whole site, filter by content type, and let Yoast AI draft metadata you approve before it saves. This update builds on that: it’s now easier to spot exactly which posts need attention, catch AI suggestions that need a second look, and get started without leaving your regular post list. 

Here’s what’s new. 

Find weak fields in seconds 

The Filters dropdown now includes “needs improvement” options for SEO title, meta description, social title, and social description. Turn one on, and the bulk editor shows only the posts where that field is empty or scoring poorly, using the same scoring your post editor already relies on. 

Once you’ve found them, you don’t have to select each one by hand. New quality-based options in the Select menu let you select every post on the page that needs improvement in a single click, using that same score, so what you filter and what you select always agree. 

Prefer working row by row? Shift+click in the Bulk Editor now selects a range at once, the way you’d expect from any table. 

Catch weak suggestions before you publish 

When you generate SEO titles, meta descriptions, or social copy in bulk, the AI does its best work with posts that already have some content to draw from. Previously, posts with very little written content could still generate suggestions, even though the input was thin, so you had no way to know which ones needed a closer look. 

That’s why the Bulk Editor now gives you a built-in guardrail: after a generation run, it flags exactly which generated posts had limited content, so you know which ones are worth a second look. Add a bit more content, regenerate, and you’re set. 

Start bulk editing from your regular post list

You no longer need to open the bulk editor separately to get started. Select posts, pages, or products from their regular overview screens, choose “Bulk edit” from the bulk actions dropdown, and your selection carries straight into the bulk editor, ready to go.

Keep working, even when your site is hard to reach (rolling out) 

If Yoast AI can’t reach your site, for example because it’s behind a firewall, offline, or has the REST API disabled, you’ll now see an option to connect your site to MyYoast right from the error message, instead of a dead end. Once connected, Yoast AI keeps working even on trickier hosting setups. This is rolling out gradually, so you may not see it yet. You don’t need to do anything to prepare, you’ll be invited to connect right when it’s useful to you.

item.content:encoded:
YMYL stands for “Your Money or Your Life.” Google holds these sites to a higher standard than other websites because the content can affect people’s finances, health, and safety. This matters because wrong information in these areas can harm real people. Google knows this. It evaluates YMYL content more strictly using its Quality Raters’ Guidelines and E-E-A-T framework (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness).

Table of contents

  • What is YMYL?
  • The importance of YMYL
  • Building user trust
  • YMYL and the Google Quality Raters’ Guidelines
  • Yoast SEO, E-E-A-T, YMYL and site policies
  • Conclusion

Key takeaways

  • YMYL stands for ‘Your Money or Your Life’ and describes content that affects people’s financial stability, health, and safety.
  • Google evaluates YMYL content with strict standards using E-E-A-T: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness.
  • AI plays a role in assessing YMYL content but still requires human oversight for accuracy.
  • Building user trust involves publishing high-quality, expert-backed content and maintaining transparency.
  • Yoast SEO Premium helps optimize YMYL sites by incorporating structured data and supporting publishing principles.

What is YMYL?

YMYL refers to websites covering topics that affect your financial stability, well-being, and quality of life. These include finance, health, safety, legal advice, and more. The common thread: readers make important decisions based on this information.

Google holds YMYL content to a higher standard because inaccurate information here can directly harm people. Search engines need to surface only reliable, expert-backed content in these areas.

Examples of YMYL topics

  • Financial advice: Investments, taxes, retirement planning, mortgages, insurance
  • Health and medical information: Medical conditions, treatments, medications, nutrition, mental health, fitness
  • Safety and emergency information: Safety instructions, disaster guidelines, emergency services
  • Legal advice: Legal information, regulations, guidance on legal matters
  • News and current affairs: Current events, politics, business, science, technology
  • Government and civics: Elections, policies, societal issues
  • AI-generated content: Google requires human review for AI-assisted YMYL content to ensure accuracy

To optimize these pages, you need to prove you deserve your readers’ trust. That means accurate information, up-to-date content, and clear expertise.

The importance of YMYL

YMYL content matters because it affects real decisions. When someone searches for medical advice or investment tips, they need answers they can rely on. Google recognizes this and sets higher quality bars for these topics.

Why do search engines focus on YMYL content?

Google focuses on YMYL because these topics influence people’s lives and financial well-being. Search engines want to surface the most trustworthy information possible. For YMYL topics, the stakes are higher. Users need information they can rely on when making important decisions.

By evaluating YMYL content more critically, Google distinguishes good sources from bad ones. This ensures users see reliable guidance, expert insights, and accurate information. Better YMYL content means better search results overall.

AI’s impact on YMYL

Google uses AI to assess YMYL content, especially for finance, health, and safety topics. AI systems evaluate content quality, fact-check claims, and prioritize trustworthy sources. However, human oversight remains essential. AI-generated YMYL content needs expert review to ensure accuracy and compliance with Google’s E-E-A-T standards. This balance keeps YMYL information reliable in search rankings.

Building user trust

You need to earn trust when publishing YMYL content. Your readers are looking for guidance on financial, health, or legal decisions. Publish high-quality, trustworthy content, and you’ll establish yourself as an authoritative source in your field.

Start with accurate information backed by experts and credible sources. Demonstrate experience, expertise, authority, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T). Keep your information up-to-date, fact-checked, and sourced. Add credentials, expert reviewers, author biographies, and external references.

When readers see your site as trustworthy, they return. They share your content. They become loyal customers or clients. Search engines also consider user trust signals, such as engagement metrics and positive reviews, when assessing YMYL content quality.

YMYL and the Google Quality Raters’ Guidelines

Google’s Quality Raters’ Guidelines help assess the quality of web pages, especially YMYL content. These guidelines show how Google evaluates E-E-A-T, which helps you optimize YMYL pages.

Insights into Google’s guidelines for YMYL pages

The Quality Raters’ Guidelines outline specific criteria for YMYL content. E-E-A-T is not a direct ranking factor. It is a framework Google uses to evaluate content quality. The guidelines focus on:

  • Experience: For finance or health topics, experience means you have worked as a financial advisor, healthcare professional, or have a background in that field.
  • Expertise: Google expects YMYL content from people or organizations with demonstrable expertise. Show this through qualifications, experience, industry recognition, and contributions to reputable publications.
  • Authoritativeness: Google gives weight to content from authoritative sources. This includes sites with established credibility, expert recognition, or a strong reputation for accurate information.
  • Trustworthiness: Trustworthiness is crucial for YMYL content. Google evaluates transparency, accuracy, and disclosure of potential biases. Sites with histories of complaints, misinformation, or malicious intent score lower.
  • Content quality: Google expects comprehensive, insightful information. Avoid shallow content. YMYL pages should satisfy user intent by addressing the main concerns and questions.

How Quality Raters assess E-E-A-T

Google’s quality raters assess experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness. While the exact process is unknown, raters evaluate several elements:

  • Qualifications and credentials: Formal education, certifications, and professional qualifications related to the topic demonstrate commitment to expertise.
  • Professional experience: Previous work experience, industry involvement, and practical expertise from specific projects or research.
  • Demonstrated knowledge and authority: Comprehensive explanations, references to reputable sources, and unique insights show depth of knowledge.
  • Industry recognition: Awards, honors, speaking invitations, and inclusion in expert lists highlight your standing.
  • User feedback and engagement: Positive feedback, active audience engagement, and a history of helpful information build trust.
  • Transparency: Disclose biases, funding sources, and other important policies to align with Google’s emphasis on authenticity.

Refining algorithms

Quality raters provide feedback to Google, which uses this to refine algorithms and improve search results. While raters do not directly influence rankings, their assessments help Google understand if everything works as intended.

Yoast SEO, E-E-A-T, YMYL and site policies

Yoast SEO helps you build your website’s E-E-A-T. As you have seen, Google assesses many factors when evaluating YMYL sites. Our plugin helps Google understand your site through structured data. Publishing principles and site policies are central to this process. In Yoast SEO Premium, you can add these pages to your structured data.

Publishing principles and site policies guide how you create and distribute content. They ensure your content is accurate, trustworthy, relevant, transparent, engaging, private, accessible, continuously improved, and legally compliant.

Structured data helps Google understand your YMYL content for AI-generated summaries and passage-level clarity. With the rise of AI Overviews, YMYL sites must prioritize structured data to improve visibility in search results.

Use schemas like publishingPrinciples to highlight your policies and expertise. This helps Google assess your credibility and relevance more effectively.

Select the pages from the fields, and you are all set. If you still need to set up these policies, now is a great time to start. They improve your website’s credibility and SEO performance.

Conclusion

To succeed with a YMYL site, focus on three things: align with Google’s guidelines, build E-E-A-T, and optimize your content. Start today by adding publishing principles and site policies in Yoast SEO Premium. Then review your author bios and make sure every YMYL article shows real expertise. item.content:encoded:
Most AI website builders promise you can create a website in minutes, but what does that timeline actually include? While AI can generate a professional-looking website surprisingly quickly, you’ll still need time to choose a domain, review the generated content, make a few edits, and publish your site. In this guide, we’ll break down the entire journey and share a realistic estimate.

Key takeaways

  • AI website builders significantly reduce the time for initial website setup, but require additional time for edits and refinements
  • Creating a basic website typically takes 30 to 90 minutes, depending on preparation, while AI can generate a first draft in about 3 minutes
  • Key stages of website creation include defining purpose, selecting a domain, and adding content, each taking varying amounts of time
  • Post-launch, focus on content updates, SEO improvements, and monitoring performance to maintain a strong online presence
  • AI tools streamline the initial setup, but successful websites still require ongoing personalization and development to truly reflect the brand

Table of contents

  • A realistic timeline: How long each stage of website creation takes
  • How AI website builders have changed the website creation timeline
  • AI builds websites quickly, but growing one still takes time
  • How much faster is building a website with AI?
  • AI gives you a head start, not the finish line

A realistic timeline: How long each stage of website creation takes

Every website follows a similar journey before it goes live. Whether you’re creating a portfolio, a business website, or an online store, you’ll need to plan your website, register a domain, set up hosting, create pages, add content, and test everything before publishing.

The time required for each stage depends on your website’s complexity, the resources you already have, and how prepared you are before you begin. The table below provides a realistic estimate of how long each stage typically takes.

Additional factors that may extend your timeline

The timeline above reflects the steps involved in building a typical website. However, certain features and functionality can add additional time depending on your requirements. For instance, if you’re building an eCommerce website or a multilingual website, the following will be added to your timeline:

Keep in mind that the estimates above focus solely on the website creation process. Some projects may require additional planning before you even begin building. For example, businesses entering a competitive market often spend extra time researching competitors, refining their brand positioning, defining their target audience, or planning their content strategy. While these activities can extend your overall timeline, they often result in a more focused website that better serves your visitors and supports your business goals.

How AI website builders have changed the website creation timeline

Traditionally, creating a website involves much more than writing content. Before you can even start customizing your site, you have to make a series of decisions that shape its overall structure and design.

The manual work AI helps you skip

Building a website from scratch typically involves tasks such as:

  • rowsing and selecting a template
  • Choosing colors and typography
  • Deciding which pages to include
  • Creating a navigation menu
  • Arranging sections on each page
  • Drafting placeholder content for your homepage and key pages

None of these tasks is particularly difficult on its own, but together they can easily add hours to the website creation process.

AI website builders shorten this setup phase by turning it into a guided onboarding experience. Instead of making every decision manually, you answer a few questions about your business, and the AI generates a website structure, page layouts, navigation, design elements, and draft content for you.

Rather than starting with a blank canvas, you start with a complete first draft that’s ready for review.

Putting AI website creation into practice

To see how this works in practice, I used the Bluehost AI Website Builder while building a website with AI from scratch.

The process was straightforward:

  • Describe the website in a single sentence
  • Create an account and verify your email address
  • Answer a few questions about your business, website goals, preferred design style, and overall tone
  • Let the AI generate the website

Once onboarding was complete, the AI produced a complete first draft in about 3 minutes. The generated website already includes:

  • A homepage
  • A navigation menu
  • Pre-designed page sections
  • AI-generated copy
  • Placeholder images based on the information provided

It’s still WordPress underneath

One feature that stood out was that the generated website wasn’t locked inside a simplified editor. Because Bluehost’s AI Website Builder is built on WordPress, I could immediately access the complete WordPress dashboard to:

  • Edit pages
  • Preview posts
  • Install plugins
  • Customize themes
  • Manage site settings

In other words, the AI accelerated the initial website setup without limiting what I could do afterward.

Where you’ll probably spend the most time

Although AI significantly reduces the time required to create the first version of a website, there are still several areas where you’ll likely invest additional time.

Refining your content

AI-generated copy provides a strong starting point, but it should reflect your products, services, brand personality, and unique value proposition. Reviewing and personalizing the content is one of the most important steps before publishing.

Choosing the right images

The first draft may include placeholders or stock images. Replacing these with your own photography, product images, or branded visuals helps create a more authentic and trustworthy website.

Expanding your website

Depending on your business, you may want to create additional pages beyond the initial draft, such as an About page, service pages, FAQs, testimonials, pricing information, or a blog. AI accelerates the initial launch, but your website can continue to grow over time.

Optimizing for search engines

Publishing your website doesn’t mean your work is finished. Optimizing page titles, meta descriptions, internal links, headings, and on-page content, as well as creating valuable blog posts, is what helps people discover your website through search engines over the long term.

While AI can dramatically reduce the time it takes to create a website, the biggest improvements usually come after the first draft. Personalizing your content, using original visuals, expanding your website with valuable pages, and continuously improving your SEO are what transform an AI-generated starting point into a website that genuinely represents your brand and stands out from the competition.

Final verdict: So, how long does it really take to build a website with AI?

If you’re wondering whether AI website builders really save time, the answer is yes, but perhaps not in the way most marketing claims suggest.

The website generation itself is remarkably quick. In my experience, the Bluehost AI Website Builder produced a complete first draft in around three minutes after the onboarding process. However, creating an account, verifying your email, answering the AI’s questions, reviewing the generated website, and making your own edits naturally add to the overall timeline.

For most people starting from scratch, it’s reasonable to expect a basic website to be online within 30 to 90 minutes, depending on how prepared you are. If you already have your domain, branding, and content ready, you could realistically publish in under 15 minutes. On the other hand, if you’re building a more polished website with custom copy, additional pages, and SEO improvements, you should expect to spend a few hours or even a full day refining it.

The biggest impact of AI isn’t that it builds a perfect website in minutes. It’s that it compresses what used to be the most time-consuming part of website creation, setting up the structure, layouts, navigation, and first draft into a guided process that takes only a few minutes. Instead of spending hours building a website from an empty canvas, you can dedicate your time to improving the content, design, and user experience, which are ultimately the elements that make a website successful.

So, are AI-generated websites any good?

For most individuals and small businesses, yes, they’re a strong starting point. AI website builders can generate a professional-looking first draft in minutes, but you’ll still get the best results by personalizing the content, visuals, and SEO to reflect your brand and goals.

AI builds websites quickly, but growing one still takes time

Once your website is live, keeping it useful, discoverable, and up to date still requires ongoing effort. AI website builders can help you create and publish a website much faster than traditional methods, but launching your website is only the beginning.

Here are a few areas to focus on after launch.

Publish helpful content regularly

Whether you’re running a business website or an online store, regularly publishing helpful content keeps your website fresh and gives people more reasons to visit. If you’re not sure where to start, check out our guide on writing an SEO-friendly blog post.

Keep your website up to date

Your website should evolve alongside your business. As your products, services, pricing, or contact information change, make sure your website reflects those updates. You can also expand your website over time by adding new landing pages, service pages, FAQs, or case studies as your business grows.

If you are using Yoast SEO, creating FAQ pages becomes very easy. The plugin’s FAQ content block converts your questions into structured data, making them easier for search engines and AI crawlers to digest.

Continue improving your SEO

Publishing your website is only the first step. To help people find your website, you’ll need to continue optimizing both your content and your website’s technical foundation.
